constraints: The policy is stable, mandatory for every request, and fits with headroom.
The question is the changing part of the request.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: The fixed policy consumes a known amount of context, but it removes retrieval variability and keeps the required authority present.
details.errorCorrection: Use progressive discovery where context or relevance requires it; keep small mandatory material in the stable core.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Static context precedes dynamic content and can be cached at an explicit breakpoint; the policy remains visible as the authority for every answer.
details.scenarioApplication: Load the current policy version before the question, label its sections and effective date, and monitor headroom as the corpus or workload changes.
details.transfer: Choose monolithic context for small, stable, universally required material and revisit the boundary when size or query selectivity changes.

messages.text: Repeated discovery adds latency and variability for material that every request requires and that fits comfortably.
General knowledge cannot replace the authoritative safety policy and its current effective version.
Optional documents add irrelevant context and reduce headroom without serving the stated mandatory-policy workload.

feedback.reason: The mandatory policy is small, stable, and needed every time, so a structured monolithic core is simpler than rediscovering it. A stable prefix may also be reused when the request pattern supports it.

options.text: Place the complete structured policy in stable context, put the changing question after it, and use a cache breakpoint when the request pattern supports it.
Rediscover the same mandatory policy paragraphs on every request so the assistant can keep the initial prompt small despite ample context headroom.
Omit the policy and use general safety knowledge, adding a manual citation after the answer if the analyst asks for authority.
Load every optional company document alongside the policy so future questions need no additional retrieval, even when those documents are irrelevant.

prompt: A small team asks repeated questions about a stable 20-page safety policy required for every answer. It fits comfortably with the system prompt and expected response. Which context boundary is proportionate?

constraints: The complete archive crowds out relevant evidence before the query narrows the working set.
The appendix must remain available as a retrievable source.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: The agent performs an additional retrieval step and can report unavailable evidence, but it avoids repeating a huge archive on every request.
details.errorCorrection: Reduce irrelevant active context while preserving the source; do not treat chance, output length, or deletion as relevance controls.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Just-in-time retrieval keeps a compact index or report map in the initial context and loads detailed sections after the query establishes relevance.
details.scenarioApplication: Return report and section metadata, fetch the matching appendix and surrounding evidence, and cite the report version and section in the answer.
details.transfer: When a complete archive causes misses, keep identifiers in context and load high-fidelity detail only after the query narrows the evidence.

messages.text: More output tokens cannot improve source selection and can increase cost while the archive still crowds out the appendix.
Reordering the same oversized archive changes presentation but keeps low-signal content competing and does not guarantee that the relevant appendix enters the working set.
Deleting a valid appendix hides the context problem and makes questions requiring it impossible to answer.

feedback.reason: The failure is context pollution and poor relevance, not a shortage of generation tokens. Lightweight identifiers allow the agent to narrow evidence while retaining the appendix for questions that need it.

options.text: Expose report IDs and metadata first, then retrieve the relevant sections and appendix just in time for the current question.
Keep the monolithic archive, raise output-token limits, and rely on a longer answer to mention the missed appendix.
Reorder the complete archive by recency or topical score on each request and rely on the new ordering to bring the missed appendix into the model's attention.
Delete the appendix because the current prompt missed it and maintain only the background sections used most often.

prompt: A research agent receives a complete archive in every request and misses a relevant appendix while repeating background text, despite a large context window. What context diagnosis should guide repair?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A small stable resource needed on every request may remain eager if measurement supports it.
details.errorCorrection: Eager resources keep the dominant cost; tool removal is unrelated; permanent summaries can lose evidence and provenance.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Discovery for tools does not automatically curate resource data.
details.scenarioApplication: Retrieve relevant resource content just in time and preserve a path to its source.
details.transfer: Manage capability metadata and content payloads as distinct context decisions.

messages.text: A permanent summary can lose details and provenance required for evidence.
The resource payload remains the dominant context cost.
Deleting tool metadata does not reduce the loaded resource content.

feedback.reason: Tool definitions and resource contents are separate context costs. Deferring only one leaves the other eager payload unchanged.

options.text: Summarize all resources once and discard original text.
Return all resources eagerly because tool discovery already reduces tokens.
Remove tools from the catalog to make resource content cheaper.
Defer definitions; separately control resource-body payloads.

prompt: A client defers tool descriptions but loads all resource contents into every prompt. Resource size now dominates context. What is the correct next adjustment?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If the headroom shrinks or discovery becomes local/prefetched, compare again; if this tool is not needed on a route, keep it out of that route.
details.errorCorrection: The low-use label does not outweigh the explicit route constraints. The evidence supports this compact tool being eager, not a rule to load the entire catalog eagerly.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Progressive disclosure has both context savings and lookup costs.
details.scenarioApplication: Keep this 500-token schema in the route’s initial definitions and measure context use and completion latency. Defer other tools only when their own context and discovery costs support it.
details.transfer: Choose eager versus deferred loading per route using schema cost, request share, discovery delay, and the SLA of sessions that need the capability.

messages.text: Deleting the tool would remove a capability used in 30% of sessions without needing to do so: its 500-token definition fits the stated headroom.
A blanket rule to defer every minority-use tool ignores that this discovery delay alone exceeds the 1.5-second SLA for affected sessions.
The numbers justify keeping this one definition eager; they do not show that all other tools fit the context budget or belong on this route.

feedback.reason: Although only 30% of sessions need the tool, the schema fits the available 800-token headroom and deferred discovery by itself exceeds their 1.5-second end-to-end SLA. Keep this definition eager on the affected route.

options.text: Delete it because one route cannot meet the SLA.
Defer it because rare tools should never be eager.
Load every tool eagerly because any discovery step adds latency to the request.
Keep this schema eager; its two-second lookup misses the route SLA.

prompt: A workflow has one minority-use tool. Its schema costs 500 tokens, the route has 800 tokens of measured context headroom, and discovering the schema adds 2 seconds only on sessions that need it. Those sessions have a 1.5-second end-to-end SLA. Which loading policy fits this route?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If measured discovery or failure handling consumes more than the 600 ms budget, re-evaluate the schema size or route contract rather than assuming deferral is always better.
details.errorCorrection: A small use share does not justify deleting an authorized capability, and eager availability is not free when it pushes required evidence out of context.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Progressive loading trades definition tokens against lookup latency; its value depends on how often the schema is needed and what evidence eager loading displaces.
details.scenarioApplication: Retain the compact universal core, discover the compliance schema on the 2% route, and test whether the 250 ms lookup fits the 600 ms headroom while eliminating the 5% missing-source failure.
details.transfer: Keep always-needed context available and load the measured minority payload when its task requires it.

messages.text: All four schemas are not universally needed, and eager loading is already displacing evidence on ordinary requests.
Low use is a context-allocation signal, not evidence that the capability can be removed.
Truncating evidence preserves the cause of the observed failure rather than fixing the loading policy.

feedback.reason: The evidence shows that eager loading displaces source material on every request, while the affected route has enough measured headroom for discovery. Defer only the minority schema and evaluate both evidence completeness and route latency.

options.text: Keep the core eager; test deferred compliance lookup against its route deadline.
Keep all four schemas eager because every tool must be available before a task begins.
Remove the compliance tool because its current use share is only 2%.
Keep the fourth schema eager and truncate user evidence to maintain a fixed prompt size.

prompt: A client has a compact core of three schemas used in every request and a 480-token compliance tool definition used by 2% of requests. Loading all four consumes the last 480 tokens reserved for user evidence on every request; those requests now omit a relevant source in 5% of cases. The compliance route has 600 ms of deadline headroom, and measured discovery adds 250 ms. Which context policy should be tested?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Retrieve the current relevant passage at the point of use and carry its revision into the answer.
details.errorCorrection: Loading the full archive wastes context; discarding sources makes verification harder.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Context compression should preserve identifiers and unresolved constraints that let a later step recover exact source material.
details.scenarioApplication: A summary is not a substitute for the current policy addendum when its version is missing.
details.transfer: Design handoffs to preserve recoverable state rather than every original token.

messages.text: The archive location helps discovery but the omitted version still leaves the receiving agent unable to establish which source is current.
A title and date are not a reliable version identity, and a search-based assumption can still select superseded policy.
A query without stable source IDs or version state can retrieve the same superseded passage again.

feedback.reason: The summary retained intent but lost the version needed to identify current authority. Stable references plus bounded just-in-time retrieval recover that evidence without loading the archive.

options.text: Include a compact policy summary and its full archive location in every handoff, then let the next agent search that archive for the applicable addendum.
Carry the previous addendum’s title and date in the summary, then reuse it unless the recipient finds a newer matching title.
Pass the selected answer and a retrieval query to the next agent, allowing it to find whichever policy version best fits the task.
Carry stable source IDs and version metadata, then retrieve the current task-relevant addendum before answering.

prompt: A handoff summary preserves the task goal and selected approach but omits the policy addendum’s version. The receiving agent answers from a superseded addendum; loading the entire 8,000-page archive into every handoff would exceed context. What should the handoff contract add?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Retrieve exact source passages at the point of use and retain their references.
details.errorCorrection: A summary may omit evidence needed to support a claim, while removing the core can lose required context.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Context allocation should account for the value of each payload, not merely document availability.
details.scenarioApplication: The policy core is used broadly; the incident record and handbook sections are task-specific.
details.transfer: Keep universal context bounded and retrieve the variable tail selectively.

messages.text: Reordering may help one known case but retains the context burden and does not provide targeted access to other relevant sections.
A refreshed synopsis may omit incident details needed for verification and is a derived replacement for source evidence.
This preserves policy but shifts the missing evidence burden to users despite the assistant having access to the handbook.

feedback.reason: The current payload displaces case-specific evidence while repeating broad context. A compact core plus targeted retrieval preserves both governing policy and the needed incident facts.

options.text: Keep the whole handbook attached but move the incident record to the front and add an instruction not to repeat the compact policy.
Keep the compact policy core available and retrieve the incident record and only the relevant handbook sections when needed.
Build a compressed handbook synopsis and use it instead of the current source sections, refreshing it on each document release.
Keep the policy core and ask users to paste the incident record when it matters, avoiding a retrieval change for now.

prompt: A support agent receives a 600-page handbook on every request. Context pressure removes the cited incident record near the end, while answers still repeat general policy already contained in a compact, current reference. What change best preserves the evidence needed for the task?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Reassess if schema size, use share, or discovery latency changes.
details.errorCorrection: Removing a required operation or eagerly loading the rare catalog does not address the measured route costs.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Progressive discovery is a measured tradeoff, not a universal rule.
details.scenarioApplication: Eager loading can be proportionate for a compact, frequently used capability while a rare large tail stays deferred.
details.transfer: Choose loading policy per route and capability using measured context and latency.

messages.text: Discovery adds 300 ms against only 500 ms remaining and the schema is used by nearly every request; this shifts avoidable latency to the common path.
Examples do not replace the schema contract and can cause malformed operation arguments.
Forty rare schemas add unneeded context and the stated compact schema already has enough headroom.

feedback.reason: The compact schema is used almost universally and fits measured headroom; its 300 ms discovery cost consumes most of the affected route’s remaining budget.

options.text: Keep this high-use compact schema eager; continue deferring the large rare schemas and monitor route context.
Defer the compact schema behind local discovery only when it is not called, then measure whether the 300 ms lookup leaves enough route margin.
Keep the schema deferred and let the model infer the typed parameters from the tool name and recent examples.
Load all schemas eagerly to avoid lookup delays, while reserving the last 20% of context for user evidence.

prompt: A route loads a compact 700-token tool schema on every request. The schema is used on 98% of requests, leaves sufficient evidence headroom, and local discovery adds 300 ms to a route with 500 ms of remaining budget. Another 40 rarely used schemas are already deferred. What should the team do with the compact schema?

constraints: The global policy is mandatory and fits as stable context.
Jurisdiction addenda are optional per request but may control the answer and must be available by metadata.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Some requests wait for addendum retrieval or escalation, but the assistant avoids 8,000 pages of irrelevant context and does not mask missing jurisdiction rules.
details.errorCorrection: Keep mandatory compact authority monolithic and discover optional controlling detail just in time with a defined unavailable state.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Stable context holds the governing core; metadata retrieves the jurisdiction/version addendum, and generation receives only relevant sections after the scope is known.
details.scenarioApplication: Resolve jurisdiction and active version, fetch the matching addendum, cite both policy layers, and route or abstain if the controlling addendum cannot be loaded.
details.transfer: For policies with a universal core and conditional addenda, combine stable context with metadata-scoped progressive retrieval and explicit failure handling.

messages.text: Loading all addenda consumes context on irrelevant jurisdictions and creates a large evidence-selection problem.
The global rule may be incomplete or overridden for the supplied jurisdiction, so answering without the addendum can be unsafe.
Semantic similarity does not guarantee jurisdiction, version, or controlling scope and can select a plausible wrong addendum.

feedback.reason: The global policy is universal and fits, while addenda are high-cardinality, jurisdiction-specific evidence. Progressive discovery narrows the addendum and makes its absence visible instead of silently answering from incomplete authority.

options.text: Keep the global policy as structured stable context, discover the matching addendum by jurisdiction and version, retrieve relevant sections, and abstain or escalate if required addendum evidence cannot load.
Load all jurisdiction addenda with the global policy so every rule is immediately visible, accepting 8,000 pages of mostly irrelevant context.
Answer from the global policy whenever the matching addendum cannot be loaded, and mention the jurisdiction only in explanatory prose.
Search all addenda semantically and choose the highest-scoring passage as the controlling rule without enforcing jurisdiction or version metadata.

prompt: A safety assistant must include a 20-page global policy in every answer, but jurisdiction addenda total 8,000 pages and only some requests need one. The question supplies a jurisdiction and addenda are indexed by jurisdiction and version. Which context design is correct?

constraints: The 20-page global policy is mandatory and fits every request.
Jurisdiction addenda total 8,000 pages, are needed only 1 in 50 requests, and are addressable by jurisdiction/version metadata.
A missing required addendum must produce an unavailable or escalation state.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If every request required all addenda or metadata could not identify the governing section, keep the required evidence or expose an explicit unavailable state.
details.errorCorrection: The addenda consume context on 49 of 50 requests and can be selected reliably from the supplied jurisdiction and version.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Progressive disclosure keeps lightweight identifiers first and loads detailed information only when relevant. The scenario's mechanism is governed by this decisive constraint: The infrequently used addenda should move to progressive disclosure while the mandatory global policy remains in stable core context.
details.scenarioApplication: Keep the global policy in the stable core, discover the jurisdiction and version addendum by metadata, load only relevant sections, and abstain or escalate if required evidence cannot be retrieved.
details.transfer: Keep mandatory common policy in context and load rare addenda by jurisdiction and version; missing required evidence must stop the answer or escalate.

messages.text: The addenda consume context on 49 of 50 requests and can be selected reliably from the supplied jurisdiction and version.
The global policy is mandatory for every answer; making it optional undermines the stated authority boundary.
Metadata can identify the relevant addendum, while loading every addendum wastes context and contradicts the rare-use evidence.

feedback.reason: The changed usage frequency and metadata make progressive loading more efficient without hiding mandatory authority.

options.text: Load all 8,000 pages up front so every answer has complete jurisdiction context.
Drop the global policy from the core and retrieve both the global policy and addendum only when the query appears to require them.
Load the matching addendum for every request and keep the full addendum set available as an always-on safety buffer.
Keep the global policy in core, load only the metadata-selected addendum, and abstain or escalate when evidence is unavailable.

prompt:
A safety assistant must include a stable 20-page global policy in every answer, but jurisdiction addenda total 8,000 pages and only one request in fifty needs an addendum. The request supplies jurisdiction and policy version.

Which context-loading policy fits the stable core and rare jurisdiction evidence?

constraints: The 12,000-token policy core and 2,000-token catalog/version map are stable monthly material used on every request.
Detailed manuals total 100,000 tokens, change daily, and are needed only after product, version, and issue are identified.
The stable prefix has a 90% hit rate, but current manual revision must be validated independently.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If a manual section became mandatory for every request and were versioned with the core, move that section before the breakpoint only after freshness and context tests.
details.errorCorrection: The manuals are not needed for most requests, change daily, and would enlarge the stable prefix; exact-prefix reuse of stable bytes does not establish that retrieved manual detail is current.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Static context can be placed before dynamic content with an explicit cache breakpoint; stable required material need not be rediscovered each request. The scenario's mechanism is governed by this decisive constraint: Keep stable required context before the breakpoint for reuse, assemble daily manual detail after routing, and validate its active revision separately; provider exact-prefix reuse must not be treated as a freshness check.
details.scenarioApplication: Place the policy core and catalog/version map before a cache breakpoint, keep manual identifiers available, load the selected active section after routing, and expose an unavailable state when detail cannot be retrieved or its current revision is not validated.
details.transfer: Put reusable stable policy and routing metadata before dynamic evidence; load only the narrowed current revision and verify freshness separately from cache reuse.

messages.text: The manuals are not needed for most requests, change daily, and exact-prefix reuse of stable bytes does not establish current manual detail.
Daily-changing detail would invalidate the stable prefix and is not needed before routing; the cache boundary should follow the stable core and map.
Cache reuse is not a freshness check for daily detail; the selected active revision must be validated and unavailable states must remain explicit.

feedback.reason: The architecture combines progressive disclosure with a cache boundary aligned to change rates while keeping current-evidence validation explicit.

options.text: Cache stable core and map before the breakpoint, load current detail after routing, and validate its revision separately.
Put the full manuals into the stable cached prompt because cache hits make repeated detailed context cheap.
Move the daily manual detail before the breakpoint so it benefits from the observed 90% hit rate, then route using the cached result.
Trust a cache hit as proof that the manual section is current and omit active revision IDs from the retrieved evidence.

prompt:
A knowledge assistant uses a stable 12,000-token policy core and a 2,000-token catalog/version map on every request. Detailed manuals total 100,000 tokens and are needed only after product, version, and issue are identified; the stable prefix currently has a 90% cache hit rate.

Which prompt layout preserves reuse while keeping daily evidence current?

constraints: The inventory exceeds useful ordinary-task context.
The long tail must remain available through governed discovery rather than deletion.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Rare requests need an extra discovery step and may incur retrieval latency, but ordinary tasks gain context headroom and fewer wrong-tool choices.
details.errorCorrection: Treat detailed capability definitions as just-in-time context and preserve a real discovery path for uncommon operations.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Lightweight names and metadata support search; the system retrieves the selected authorized tool schema before invocation so the model has the contract it needs.
details.scenarioApplication: Keep common capability identifiers visible, search the catalog for an approved task, hydrate only the selected definitions, and recheck authorization before use.
details.transfer: When an inventory is larger than ordinary context, use progressive disclosure with complete schemas at invocation rather than eager bloat or deletion.

messages.text: Eager loading recreates the context pressure and selection competition that caused the observed failures.
Frequency does not prove a capability is obsolete; deletion removes legitimate behavior instead of managing its context cost.
Loading the schema only after an invocation error leaves required parameters and constraints unavailable before execution.

feedback.reason: A large eager inventory consumes context and creates selection ambiguity, while deletion loses valid long-tail behavior. Progressive discovery keeps a small initial surface and loads contracts when relevant.

options.text: Load all tool definitions at startup, add a relevance instruction to the system prompt, and rely on model selection to suppress capabilities that are unrelated to the current task.
Load lightweight discovery identifiers first and expand only the detailed definitions needed for the current capability and authorized task.
Delete uncommon tools from the enterprise catalog so the model never has to choose among rare capabilities.
Expose lightweight tool names and invoke the selected operation using model-inferred arguments, loading its detailed schema only after an invocation error.

prompt: An enterprise assistant can access 2,000 tools, but most tasks use fewer than five. Loading all definitions leaves little room for user documents and causes similar tools to be selected incorrectly. Which context strategy is appropriate?

constraints: A compact catalog map is required for every routing decision.
Detailed manuals should enter context only after product, version, and issue are narrowed.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: The answer may need a second retrieval and can be unavailable when detail is missing, but the assistant avoids a bloated prompt and random evidence.
details.errorCorrection: Separate routing context from detailed evidence and make discovery and unavailable states explicit.
details.mechanismOrProperty: A stable catalog core supplies identifiers and versions; progressive retrieval loads relevant sections just in time and reports when a required manual is unavailable.
details.scenarioApplication: Resolve product and active version from the map, retrieve the issue section and references, and cite the manual revision or escalate if it cannot be loaded.
details.transfer: For moderately sized catalogs, keep a compact stable routing core and progressively load authoritative detail after query narrowing.

messages.text: All manuals up front consume context and erase the distinction between universal routing information and request-specific detail.
Similarity ranking without the catalog overview can select a wrong product or version and leaves the authoritative routing metadata for generation to infer.
Loading all manuals before narrowing wastes context and asks generation to infer metadata that the catalog can provide directly.
Without the stable map, every request loses the product and version routing signal that can narrow detailed retrieval.
Without just-in-time manual retrieval and an unavailable state, the assistant either bloats context or appears complete without required detail.

feedback.reason: The compact map is universal routing context, while full manuals are high-cardinality detail that becomes relevant only after the query narrows scope. Both choices preserve evidence without filling ordinary context.

options.text: Include every full manual up front so the assistant can answer any issue without a second retrieval step.
Keep the catalog overview and version map in the stable core so every request can identify the relevant product and active version.
Hide the overview, select a manual from a similarity-ranked sample, and let the model infer product and version from that selected document.
Ask the model to infer the product and version from the full manuals after they have all been loaded.
Retrieve selected manual sections and references only after product, version, and issue are narrowed, preserving an explicit unavailable state when detail cannot load.

prompt: A knowledge assistant serves a moderately sized stable catalog. Its overview and version map help every request, while full manuals are needed only after product, version, and issue are identified. Which TWO context choices fit? Select TWO.
